newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection starts in du Pont murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection starts in du Pont murder trial.

text.p: Jury selection began on Tuesday in the murder trial of multimillionaire chemical heir John du Pont, accused of killing Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz nearly one year ago.

Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins began questioning a pool of 75 potential jurors in the trial, which she said was expected to take about a month. A total of 12 jurors and six alternates will be chosen.

Du Pont, 58, faced the group from the front of the courtroom, his drawn face framed by shaggy gray hair and beard. He wore a dark blue sweatsuit emblazoned in yellow with the name of the Foxcatcher wrestling team he sponsored at his estate in suburban Philadelphia, where Schultz was killed. Du Pont was accompanied by his three lawyers.
Schultz's widow, Nancy, sat near prosecutors on the other side of the courtroom. She is expected to be present for the course of the trial.

In describing the case to the potential jurors, Jenkins said, "the commonwealth alleges that on Jan. 26, 1996 ... the defendant shot David Schultz multiple times, resulting in his death." Schultz and his family lived on the Foxcatcher estate where he worked as a coach at a training facility.

Lawyers for du Pont, who has been quoted as describing himself as the Dalai Lama and the Christ child, have said they would use an insanity defence. Du Pont, charged with first- and third-degree murder and related offences, faces an automatic life sentence if convicted of first-degree murder.
Jenkins has imposed a limited gag order on the case and barred both defence and prosecution lawyers from making any comment during the selection process.

Initial questions in the jury selection focused on issues such as whether any of the jurors knew or worked for du Pont, had experience in cases where the insanity defence was used or had a connection to the case that could cloud their judgment.

Jenkins said jurors would not be sequestered during the trial but she told the potential jurors they would have to avoid all news coverage of the trial. She said she would provide them with summaries after the trial was over.
